transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-15 16:00 UTC | Duration: 49m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Khalid (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (Redwood SA); Lena Ortiz (CTO), Daniel Park (Head Infra), Rajesh Menon (Head Security), Priya Rao (SRE), Tom Whittaker (PM)
--- Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial) ---
Summary: talk about failovers, reroute policies, canary fallbacks, and what determines SLA credits.
--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick round — can you confirm we have the right folks on the line?
[00:06] Lena Ortiz: yep this is lena, i'm the cto, daniel and rajesh are here.
[00:11] Daniel Park: yep
[00:12] Rajesh Menon: morning all
[00:14] Maya Chen: great. today we want to understand your reliability goals and constraints — especially around incident tolerance and how you'd want Redwood to failover.
[00:23] Tom Whittaker: high level — we handle PHI, regulatory, so we need deterministic failover windows and audit trails. we also care about cost though, so we might not want two fully hot regions all the time.
[00:34] Omar Khalid: totally — that's the classic hot-hot vs hot-warm tradeoff. we typically propose a few patterns: single-region hosted with cross-region read-only fallback; active-active multi-region with active routing; dedicated pools per region; or private deployments inside your VPC with replicated control planes.
[00:52] Priya Rao: can you clarify the difference in practice between hosted and dedicated for failover? like, if us-east goes down what happens?
[01:00] Omar Khalid: good question. for Hosted API, we have automatic routing policies that prefer region-local endpoints, and on capacity or region outage we apply policy-based fallback — that might be routing to another region with compatible model variants. there is a brief cold-start window if a model variant wasn't warm — we can pre-warm for you for critical endpoints.
[01:21] Rajesh Menon: when you say "compatible model variant" — do you mean quantized model differences or completely different model architecture? we need output determinism for clinical decision support.
[01:31] Jared Liu: right, so we try to fall back to the same model version if available elsewhere. if not, we fall back to a verified compatible variant (for example 8-bit quantized vs 16-bit fp16) — outputs can differ slightly, we track a regression matrix. for clinical we recommend pinning versions and enabling strict rollout policies and also having a blackbox check against a golden prompt set.
[01:51] Daniel Park: and latency during fallback — what are we looking at? we can't have 3-5s spikes for patient-facing flows.
[01:58] Omar Khalid: target SLO for cross-region failover is configurable. typical numbers: warm region failover <300ms extra p95; cold start pre-warmed it's sub-100ms; cold model spin-up could be several 100s ms to low seconds depending on sequence length and model. in Dedicated we can reserve standby capacity to guarantee sub-200ms.
[02:23] Lena Ortiz: can you explain standby vs reserve — we want to avoid paying for full duplication if possible.
[02:29] Maya Chen: sure — standby means you pay for minimal reserved GPU resources that can be scaled quickly; reserve means fully reserved right away and you pay commit. we can do burst policies where you pay a low baseline and a quick-burst to full capacity only during incidents.
[02:46] Priya Rao: what's the SLA commitment for hosted vs dedicated?
[02:50] Omar Khalid: Hosted: typically 99.9% platform availability, with token-level throttling and best-effort cross-region routing. Dedicated comes with SLA options up to 99.95% depending on commit and on-call tier. Private (VPC) SLAs are contractual and tied to managed support levels; on-prem has different terms. credits are standard — we publish an SLA doc.
[03:12] Rajesh Menon: how is the failover initiated — DNS TTL, LB health checks, or application-level retries? we have strict requirements for RTO.
[03:21] Omar Khalid: we use a mix: edge routing with low TTL plus in-region health checks and an application-aware router that can route based on policy. customers can choose DNS-based failover, anycast (for low-latency), or client-side SDK that will automatically reach for an alternative endpoint. we also support a control-plane policy that will perform automated rollbacks to last known-good model when error rates spike.
[03:45] Tom Whittaker: anycast worries me because of sticky sessions and cache warming.
[03:50] Jared Liu: correct — anycast helps with latency but makes warm KV/ prefix cache harder. for model KV cache we recommend session affinity or token-aware routing in active-active setups. otherwise you see cold-cache penalty.
[04:03] Daniel Park: what's the expected token cost during failover spikes?
[04:07] Maya Chen: costs can rise due to cold starts and duplicated requests. Redwood Optimize offers intelligent caching and request dedupe to reduce duplicate token costs, and we can set policies to throttle or degrade gracefully (e.g., shorter generation length) to keep unit cost bounded during incidents.
[04:24] Priya Rao: observability — we need traceability down to prompt-level inputs and token-level cost accounting for audits.
[04:31] Omar Khalid: we expose per-request trace IDs, token breakdowns, latency histograms, and full request/response logs configurable with retention. for PHI we recommend sending only metadata to Redwood logs and using customer-side encrypted payloads or private deployment to keep raw PHI in your VPC.
[04:52] Rajesh Menon: KMS/HSM — is there a managed option?
[04:55] Maya Chen: yes, we have integrations with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM-backed keystores for private deployments. Hosted customers can use Redwood-managed encryption but for compliance we recommend a customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or Private.
[05:08] Lena Ortiz: do you support audit logging for model rollouts, who triggered a fallback, and traceable canary decisions?
[05:15] Jared Liu: yes — console tracks rollout history, canary metrics, who triggered rollbacks; we also keep an immutable audit trail for config changes if you enable the compliance tier.
[05:24] Tom Whittaker: in an incident who owns the escalation? if a region has network partition do we call Redwood or you call us?
[05:31] Maya Chen: we have a joint runbook model. for Dedicated and Private there is an on-call contact and we have a shared incident bridge. for Hosted we operate the platform and will notify customers, but customers with Dedicated/Private get a named SRE/CSM escalation path.
[05:45] Priya Rao: curious about experimental scenario — failover mid-ongoing session where KV cache contains patient context. what's the recommended approach?
[05:53] Omar Khalid: recommended is deterministic session reconciliation: persist KV cache to a cross-region low-latency store (we support a geo-replicated KV) or send session snapshot to customer store. on failover, Redwood can replay KV or rehydrate from snapshot. if you must not replicate PHI off-prem, you can keep snapshot in your VPC and we request it on failover.
[06:15] Daniel Park: any limitations on sequence length or model sharding during failover?
[06:19] Jared Liu: large sequence lengths can increase recovery window because of KV size; we recommend truncated context for high-availability flows or pinning shorter contexts for critical endpoints. model sharding is transparent to the API but can affect cold-start timings if replica placement differs.
[06:36] Lena Ortiz: how do you test your fallback policies — can we run a simulated region outage?
[06:41] Omar Khalid: yes we recommend a staged failure test. Redwood can orchestrate a simulated degrade: stop warmers, throttle a region, and measure client experience. that's part of our recommended benchmark plan.
[06:53] Rajesh Menon: about SLA credits — how are they computed, and do they consider partial degradation?
[06:58] Maya Chen: SLA credits are computed against measured availability and error budget; partial degradation (increased latency or partial errors) is considered in our SLO tiers and we have granular credit logic. we will share the SLA formula in the docs.
[07:10] Tom Whittaker: do you support a per-route SLO? e.g., encrypting, sensitive endpoints more strict.
[07:15] Jared Liu: yes, per-route configs are supported — you can set different rollout and fallback policies per route and different SLOs, which will be reflected in cost and billing.
[07:24] Priya Rao: what about multi-tenant isolation inside Dedicated — can teams share clusters without noisy neighbor?
[07:29] Omar Khalid: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools. within a single pool you can pin models to nodes and we provide tenant QoS controls. for strict isolation you can provision separate dedicated pools.
[07:40] Lena Ortiz: ok, let's talk about the pilot. we want a 6-week run where one critical endpoint has active-active across us-east-1 and eu-west-1, with a warm standby in ap-south-1. we want metrics on failover latency and token cost delta. can Redwood do that?
[07:56] Maya Chen: yes, that's a common pilot. we'll propose a dedicated pool for the two active regions and configure warmers in ap-south-1. Omar will draft the benchmark and runbook.
[08:06] Daniel Park: what logs will be available during pilot for debugging?
[08:09] Omar Khalid: request/response logs, tail-based sampling of token traces, cost breakdowns, per-route latency and error rates, and health metrics. all accessible via console and via a secure S3 export for retention.
[08:22] Rajesh Menon: retention windows — for compliance we need 7 years for audit trails. does Redwood store that?
[08:28] Jared Liu: we offer configurable retention; hosted's default is shorter but enterprise compliance tier supports long-term retention via customer-managed storage exports. for PHI we recommend Private with your archival pipeline.
[08:39] Tom Whittaker: about rollback automation — can we automatically revert to prior model if error rate passes X threshold?
[08:45] Omar Khalid: yes, automated rollback with configurable thresholds, and we can also auto-invoke a fallback model. automated mitigation policies are part of rollout settings.
[08:55] Priya Rao: are runbooks editable? can we tie our pager duty into Redwood incidents?
[08:59] Maya Chen: yes to both. runbooks are editable, and we support integration with PagerDuty, Opsgenie, or your internal systems.
[09:06] Lena Ortiz: what's the minimal test set you need to validate fallback correctness?
[09:10] Jared Liu: we'd want a golden prompt set of 50-200 prompts representing critical flows, and a corresponding pass/fail threshold. we'd also want end-to-end latency experiments and a load profile sample for realistic request concurrency.
[09:24] Daniel Park: about encryption in transit when cross-region — do you support mutual TLS between regions?
[09:29] Omar Khalid: yes, mTLS supported for private links and Dedicated peering; also we support signed requests for hosted endpoints.
[09:36] Rajesh Menon: any known failure modes customers should prepare for?
[09:40] Jared Liu: things we've seen: cold-cache penalties, model variant regressions, cross-region network partitions causing split-brain routing if TTLs are poorly tuned. recommended mitigations: session affinity, pre-warmers, short TTLs on edge, and golden-prompts monitoring.
[09:58] Tom Whittaker: can you demo the console's incident timeline in the deep dive?
[10:02] Maya Chen: yes — we'll include that in the SE-led session.
[10:05] Priya Rao: one more question — how are data-subject deletion requests handled across replicas?
[10:09] Omar Khalid: we propagate deletion requests to all replicas; for private deployments you control the deletion path. for hosted, we provide API to mark and purge data and provide deletion proof if needed.
[10:19] Lena Ortiz: ok, sounds good. let's capture responsibilities and who does what next.
[10:24] Maya Chen: recap — Redwood: send SOC2 & ISO pack, draft benchmark/runbook, propose pricing for Dedicated pilot. Polaris: share sample traffic, define golden prompts and SLO targets.
[10:34] Daniel Park: i'll get the sample traffic and SLOs by friday.
[10:37] Priya Rao: and i'll assemble golden prompt set.
[10:40] Rajesh Menon: security will review the pack and follow up after the deep dive.
[10:44] Maya Chen: perfect. thanks everybody — we'll follow up with calendar invite for the technical deep dive and attach the security docs in the email.
[10:52] Lena Ortiz: thanks all
[10:53] meeting ended
